headline: Record King Tides plus a big incoming swell bring moderate to major, locally extreme coastal flooding through Friday morning (worst Thursday), while land stays dry and turns warm and breezy with Santa Ana winds Thursday and Friday; light rain is possible Sunday night into Monday, and a potentially soaking storm follows next Tuesday and Wednesday.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: The rest of Tuesday night and Wednesday stay dry along the coast and in the valleys as a low-pressure system aloft nudges the warm high pressure off to the east, bringing more high clouds that clear Wednesday afternoon and evening. Wednesday's highs stay within a few degrees of Tuesday's. Northeast winds pick up below the mountain passes Wednesday afternoon and evening, gusting roughly 30–40 mph.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: On Thanksgiving (Thursday) high pressure rebuilds and winds turn offshore, bringing weak to locally moderate Santa Ana winds Thursday and Friday, strongest Thursday, with gusts of 35–45 mph in the mountains, foothills and passes (45 mph mainly in the usual windy spots). Thursday and Friday are the warmest days, 5–15 degrees above average and warmest Friday, with highs in the mid to upper 70s to mid 80s west of the mountains. Saturday stays dry and cools from Friday but is still 5–12 degrees above average.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: More noticeable cooling arrives early next week as a persistent dip in the jet stream settles over the western U.S. The first rain chance has slipped to Sunday night and Monday and looks mostly light, with snow only above 8,000 feet. A stronger storm next Tuesday (Dec 1) and Wednesday (Dec 2) could bring more substantial rain, stronger winds and continued cool weather, though timing and amounts are uncertain: the chance of 1 inch or more is 55–65 percent for the coast and valleys and 75–85 percent for the mountains, the chance of 2 inches or more is about 25–35 percent for the coast and valleys and 45–55 percent for the San Bernardino County mountains, and those mountains have a 5–10 percent chance of 5 inches or more.

coast: Coastal flooding is the big story this week on the Orange County and San Diego County coasts. Record-breaking morning high tides of 7.9–8.3 feet are expected each day through Thursday, peaking Wednesday, running about 1.1–1.2 feet above normal predictions and likely breaking the all-time records just set in late October. Surf stays around 2–5 feet through Wednesday morning, then a long-period west swell (7–8 feet every 16–18 seconds) arrives late Wednesday into Thursday, bringing 6–8 foot breakers Thursday with sets of 10–12 feet on exposed west-facing beaches, easing to 3–7 feet Friday. A Coastal Flood Warning runs until 1 PM Friday for moderate to major flooding, with locally extreme flooding expected at Thursday morning's high tide, and a High Surf Advisory covers the San Diego County coast from 1 PM Wednesday to 4 AM Friday. For boaters, no hazards are expected through early Wednesday; a Small Craft Advisory covers the outer waters (10–60 miles out from San Mateo Point to the Mexican border, including San Clemente Island) from 10 AM Wednesday to 10 AM Thursday for combined seas of 8–12 feet, with northwest gusts near 23 mph far offshore Wednesday afternoon and seas falling below 10 feet by Thursday evening.
watch_for: Moderate to major, locally extreme coastal flooding at the morning high tides through Friday, worst Thursday morning when record tides meet 10–12 foot surf sets.
Santa Ana gusts of 35–45 mph near the mountains and passes Thursday and Friday, with highs into the mid 80s west of the mountains.
Rain timing: light rain Sunday night into Monday, then a possibly soaking storm next Tuesday and Wednesday.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in the dry, warm, breezy weather through Saturday and in the record tides and coastal flooding; confidence is low on the details of rain early next week, with timing and amounts for the Tuesday–Wednesday storm still uncertain.
